items.name: Anatomy
items.description: the scientific study of the body's structures, involving observation, analysis, and dissection to understand physical attributes and relationships between body parts. From the Greek roots "ana" meaning "to cut apart" and "tomia" meaning "to cut."

items.name: Gross Anatomy
items.description: considers large structures that can be seen in the body without magnification.

items.name: Microscopic Anatomy
items.description: includes cytology and histology, requiring microscopes for observation.

items.name: Cytology
items.description: study of cells.

items.name: Histology
items.description: study of tissues.

items.name: Human Physiology
items.description: focuses on the functions of the body's structures, studying the chemistry and physics behind how these structures collaborate to sustain life functions. Emphasizes homeostasis. Specializations include neurophysiology, cardiovascular, digestive, endocrine.

groups.name: Application of Anatomy & Physiology to Nursing Practice

items.name: Assessment and Diagnosis
items.description: used to evaluate patient symptoms, identify the underlying cause of illness, and develop accurate nursing diagnoses.

items.name: Treatment Selection and Implementation
items.description: understanding how medications and treatments affect the body allows nurses to choose the most appropriate interventions and monitor for side effects.

items.name: Patient Education
items.description: nurses can explain the rationale for treatments and interventions to patients and families, promoting understanding and adherence to treatment plans.

items.name: Patient Safety
items.description: helps nurses recognize potential complications and intervene effectively.

items.name: Increased Confidence
items.description: to make informed decisions and provide expert care.

groups.name: Levels of Organization (6 Levels, Increasing in Complexity)

items.name: Chemical Level
items.description: atoms and molecules form the foundation.

items.name: Cellular Level
items.description: cells, the basic units of life, perform specific functions & perform communication.

items.name: Tissue Level
items.description: groups of similar cells with a shared function, such as muscle tissue or nervous tissue.

items.name: Organ Level
items.description: structures made up of different tissues working together, like the heart or brain.

items.name: Organ System Level
items.description: groups of organs that cooperate to perform a complex function, such as the digestive system or the cardiovascular system.

items.name: Organismal Level
items.description: the entire living individual, representing the highest level of organization.

items.name: Integumentary System (Skin)
items.description: encloses internal body structures; site of many sensory receptors. Organs: hair, skin, nails

items.name: Skeletal System (Bone)
items.description: supports the body; enables movement (with muscular system). Organs: cartilage, bones, joints

items.name: Muscular System (Muscle)
items.description: enables movement (with skeletal system); helps maintain body temperature. Organs: skeletal muscles, tendons

items.name: Nervous System (Nerves)
items.description: detects and processes sensory information; activates bodily responses. Organs: brain, spinal cord, peripheral nerves

items.name: Cardiovascular System (Heart)
items.description: delivers oxygen and nutrients to tissues; equalizes temperature in the body. Organs: heart, blood vessels

items.name: Endocrine System (Hormones)
items.description: secretes hormones; regulates bodily processes. Organs: pituitary gland, thyroid gland, pancreas, adrenal glands, testes, ovaries

items.name: Digestive System (Stomach/Colon)
items.description: processes food for use by the body; removes wastes from undigested food. Organs: stomach, liver, gallbladder, large intestine, small intestine

items.name: Urinary System (Kidneys)
items.description: controls water balance in the body; removes wastes from blood and excretes them. Organs: kidneys, urinary bladder

items.name: Lymphatic System (Immune System)
items.description: returns fluid to blood; defends against pathogens. Organs: thymus, lymph nodes, spleen, lymphatic vessels

items.name: Respiratory System (Lungs)
items.description: removes carbon dioxide from the body; delivers oxygen to blood. Organs: nasal passage, trachea, lungs

items.name: Male Reproductive System
items.description: produces sex hormones and gametes; delivers gametes to female. Organs: epididymis, testes

items.name: Female Reproductive System
items.description: produces sex hormones and gametes; supports embryo/fetus until birth; produces milk for infant. Organs: mammary glands, ovaries, uterus

items.name: Homeostasis
items.description: the maintenance of stable internal conditions within living organisms. The body maintains stability by monitoring internal conditions. Parameters like body temperature and blood pressure are tightly controlled.

items.name: Set Point
items.description: normal value (e.g., body temperature at 37°C). Parameters fluctuate slightly around this set point.

items.name: Stimulus
items.description: changes the variable; conditions in the body change from the set point.

items.name: Receptors
items.description: detect deviations from the set point.

items.name: Control Center
items.description: the brain's control centers receive information, compare it to the set point, and signal effector organs.

items.name: Effectors
items.description: organs that adjust the body's response when signaled by the control centers.

items.name: Negative Feedback (Reverses)
items.description: reverses a deviation from the set point and in turn maintains body parameters within their normal range. Continuous process in our body at all times! More common than positive feedback.

items.name: Negative Feedback Loop Steps
items.description: conditions in the body change from set point → change detected → corrective mechanisms activated → conditions returned to set point → corrective mechanisms switched off.

items.name: Negative Feedback Example (Blood Glucose)
items.description: receptors on pancreatic β-cells detect blood glucose → pancreas β-cells release insulin into bloodstream → liver takes up glucose and stores as glycogen → response decreases stimulus. Receptor: pancreatic β-cells · Control center: pancreas β-cells · Effector: liver

items.name: Positive Feedback (Amplifies)
items.description: intensifies a physiological change rather than reversing it, leading to further deviation from the normal range.

items.name: Positive Feedback Examples
items.description: oxytocin release during childbirth; milk ejection during breastfeeding; blood clotting after a cut. Breastfeeding: prolactin = milk production · oxytocin = milk ejection

items.name: Anatomical Position
items.description: standardized posture for viewing the body with precision; used as a reference point to describe body structures and positions. Upright stance · feet at shoulder width, parallel, pointing forward · upper limbs extended to the sides · palms facing forward (supinated)

items.name: Midline
items.description: divides the body into mirrored symmetrical halves.

items.name: Right / Left
items.description: refers to the body's own right and left side (R / L), not the viewer's.

items.name: Supine
items.description: lying face up, on the back.

items.name: Prone
items.description: lying face down, on the stomach.

items.name: Sagittal Plane (Lateral)
items.description: divides body into right and left sides.

items.name: Midsagittal (Median) Plane
items.description: runs down the body's center.

items.name: Parasagittal Plane
items.description: unequal division into right and left.

items.name: Frontal Plane (Coronal)
items.description: separates front and back portions.

items.name: Transverse Plane (Horizontal)
items.description: divides the body into upper and lower sections, producing cross-sectional images.

groups.name: Directional Terms (One Thing Relative to Another)

items.name: Superior / Cranial
items.description: towards the head end of the body.

items.name: Inferior / Caudal
items.description: away from the head, e.g., foot.

items.name: Anterior / Ventral
items.description: front of the body.

items.name: Posterior / Dorsal
items.description: back of the body.

items.name: Medial
items.description: towards the middle; closer to the midline.

items.name: Lateral
items.description: away from the midline. e.g., the arm is lateral to the sternum

items.name: Proximal
items.description: towards the trunk or point of origin of a part. e.g., hip is proximal to knee · femur is proximal to tibia · shoulder is proximal to elbow

items.name: Distal
items.description: away from the trunk or point of origin of a part. e.g., toes are distal to knee · fibula is distal to femur · fingers are distal to shoulder

items.name: Superficial / Deep
items.description: used inside the body; superficial = closer to the body surface, deep = farther from the surface.

items.name: Dorsal Cavity
items.description: includes the cranial and spinal (vertebral) cavities.

items.name: Ventral Cavity
items.description: includes the thoracic and abdominopelvic cavities and their subdivisions.

items.name: Thoracic Cavity
items.description: above the diaphragm; includes the superior mediastinum, pleural cavities, and pericardial cavity within the mediastinum.

items.name: Abdominopelvic Cavity
items.description: below the diaphragm; includes the abdominal cavity and pelvic cavity.

items.name: Upper Row
items.description: Right hypochondriac · Epigastric · Left hypochondriac

items.name: Middle Row
items.description: Right lumbar · Umbilical · Left lumbar

items.name: Lower Row
items.description: Right iliac · Hypogastric · Left iliac

items.name: RUQ
items.description: Right upper quadrant

items.name: LUQ
items.description: Left upper quadrant

items.name: RLQ
items.description: Right lower quadrant

items.name: LLQ
items.description: Left lower quadrant

items.name: Atoms
items.description: the smallest and most fundamental unit of matter. Consists of a nucleus (protons and neutrons) surrounded by electrons.

items.name: Molecules
items.description: chemical structures formed by at least two atoms held together by chemical bonds. e.g., water (H₂O)

items.name: Macromolecules
items.description: large molecules formed by combining smaller units called monomers. e.g., DNA – contains the instructions for the functioning of the organism

items.name: Proteins
items.description: perform various functions within organisms.

items.name: Carbohydrates
items.description: provide energy and structural support.

items.name: Lipids
items.description: store energy and make up cell membranes.

items.name: Organelles
items.description: aggregates of biomolecules surrounded by membranes within cells. e.g., mitochondria – produce ATP (energy)

items.name: Cells
items.description: the smallest fundamental unit of structure in living organisms. All living things are made of cells.

items.name: Tissues
items.description: group of similar cells carrying out the same function. e.g., muscle, nervous, epithelial and connective tissue

items.name: Organs
items.description: collections of two or more tissue types grouped together based on a common function. e.g., heart (includes muscle tissue, nervous tissue)

items.name: Organ Systems
items.description: higher level of organization consisting of functionally related organs. e.g., circulatory system – transports blood throughout the body; includes the heart and blood vessels

items.name: Organisms
items.description: individual living entities.

groups.name: Chemical Level: Matter, Elements and Atoms

items.name: Matter
items.description: the substance of the universe, from a grain of sand to a star. Exists in three states: solid, liquid, gas

items.name: Elements
items.description: matter composed of atoms that have the same number of positive charges in their nuclei. All matter is composed of elements. More than 100 elements exist, but only about 25 are required by living organisms.

items.name: Four Main Elements (about 96% of body weight)
items.description: Oxygen (O) 65.0% · Carbon (C) 18.5% · Hydrogen (H) 9.5% · Nitrogen (N) 3.2%

items.name: Other Elements in the Body
items.description: Calcium (Ca) 1.5% · Phosphorus (P) 1.0% · Potassium (K) 0.4% · Sulfur (S) 0.3% · Sodium (Na) 0.2% · Chlorine (Cl) 0.2% · Magnesium (Mg) 0.1%

items.name: Trace Elements
items.description: present in tiny amounts (less than 1.0%); essential for life. Boron, chromium, cobalt, copper, fluorine, iodine, iron, manganese, molybdenum, selenium, silicon, tin, vanadium, zinc

items.name: Atom
items.description: smallest unit of an element with that element's unique properties.

items.name: Protons
items.description: carry a positive electrical charge.

items.name: Neutrons
items.description: carry no electrical charge.

items.name: Electrons
items.description: carry a negative electrical charge.

items.name: Cells
items.description: the basic units of structure and function in the human body. You developed from a single fertilized egg cell into an organism with trillions of cells. Cell structures reflect their specialized functions.

items.name: Nucleus
items.description: the part that contains the genetic information and controls all protein synthesis; the control center of the cell. Most adult cells have one nucleus. Mature red blood cells do not have a nucleus.

items.name: Cytoplasm
items.description: the inside of the cell is divided into two compartments, the nucleus and the cytoplasm; the cytoplasm holds the organelles.

items.name: Cell Membrane
items.description: the cell's "security gate"; surrounds and protects the cell and controls what can enter and leave. This control helps the cell maintain a stable internal environment.

items.name: Selectively Permeable
items.description: allows some substances through while blocking others.

items.name: Phospholipid Bilayer
items.description: two layers of phospholipids; what the cell membrane is mainly made of.

items.name: Channels (membrane proteins)
items.description: allow certain substances to move through the membrane.

items.name: Receptors (membrane proteins)
items.description: receive signals, such as hormones. Other membrane proteins help support and identify the cell.

items.name: Mitochondria
items.description: produce ATP (energy).

items.name: Ribosomes
items.description: sites of protein synthesis. Fixed and free

items.name: Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER)
items.description: network of membranes in cytosol.

items.name: Rough ER (RER)
items.description: fixed ribosomes on surface.

items.name: Smooth ER (SER)
items.description: no ribosomes; site of lipid and steroid synthesis.

items.name: Golgi Apparatus
items.description: a series of flat membrane sacs; puts finishing touches on protein after synthesis on RER and packages protein in Golgi membrane. Finishes the protein by adding or removing sugars, such as glucose, depending on its final destination.

items.name: Secretory Vesicle
items.description: a completed protein wrapped in a bit of Golgi membrane; moves toward the cell membrane and is secreted from the cell.

items.name: Lysosomes
items.description: break down waste for "housekeeping" within the cell.

items.name: Cytoskeleton
items.description: composed of microfilaments and microtubules; provides intracellular shape and support.

items.name: Centrioles
items.description: rod-shaped structures; help separate chromosomes during mitosis.

items.name: Microvilli
items.description: tiny projections of the membrane of the absorptive cell. Seen through a light microscope, they form a fuzzy line called the brush border (e.g., small intestine).

items.name: Cilia
items.description: short, hair-like projections; wavelike motions move substances across the cell's surface.

items.name: Flagella
items.description: whip-like: thicker, longer, and fewer in number than cilia; enable sperm to swim.

items.name: Passive Transport
items.description: "downhill" movement (no ATP needed). Diffusion · facilitated diffusion · osmosis · tonicity · filtration

items.name: Active Transport
items.description: "uphill" movement that requires ATP. Active transport pumps · endocytosis · exocytosis

items.name: Diffusion
items.description: movement of a substance from an area of higher concentration to one of lower concentration. e.g., oxygen and carbon dioxide moving between the alveoli and blood

items.name: Equilibrium
items.description: point at which concentration is equal and no further net diffusion occurs.

items.name: Facilitated Diffusion
items.description: a helper molecule within the membrane assists with the movement of substances from higher to lower concentration. e.g., glucose being "helped" downhill

items.name: Osmosis
items.description: movement of water (solvent) from area with more water to area with less water, across a selectively permeable membrane.

items.name: Tonicity
items.description: ability of a solution to affect the volume and pressure within a cell; describes the solute concentration of the surrounding fluid and determines the direction of water movement.

items.name: Isotonic Solution
items.description: water movement is balanced. e.g., normal saline – cell keeps its shape

items.name: Hypotonic Solution
items.description: water moves into the cell (passive transport/osmosis). e.g., water – cell swells

items.name: Hypertonic Solution
items.description: water moves out of the cell. e.g., concentrated salt solution – cell shrinks

items.name: Filtration
items.description: movement of water and dissolved substances from an area of higher pressure to an area of lower pressure; they are pushed. e.g., force from the heart pushes water out of blood vessels

items.name: Active Transport Pumps
items.description: move substance from area of lower concentration to area of higher concentration; require input of energy (ATP).

items.name: Endocytosis
items.description: ingestion of substances by the cell membrane. Phagocytosis (cell eating) · pinocytosis (cell drinking)

items.name: Exocytosis
items.description: secretion of cellular products out of the cell.

groups.name: Cell Division, Stem Cells and Differentiation

items.name: Cell Division (Cell Reproduction)
items.description: cells have a limited life span, so cellular division is necessary for bodily growth and repair. Skin, bone marrow, and digestive tract lining cells reproduce rapidly; some nerve cells do not reproduce at all.

items.name: Mitosis
items.description: a single cell divides into two genetically identical daughter cells (2n → 2n). Primary functions: growth, tissue repair, and asexual reproduction

items.name: Meiosis
items.description: a cell divides into four genetically unique daughter cells, each with half the chromosome number of the parent (2n → n). Sole function: produce gametes (sperm and eggs) for sexual reproduction

items.name: Cell Cycle
items.description: the sequence of events that a cell goes through from one mitotic division to the next.

items.name: Stem Cells
items.description: relatively undifferentiated or unspecialized cells whose only function is the production of additional unspecialized cells. Rate of division varies with tissue type; stem cells in bone marrow and skin can divide more than once a day.

items.name: Cell Differentiation
items.description: an unspecialized cell becomes a specialized cell (e.g., neuron, red blood cell, muscle, bone, epithelial cell) as enzymes are "switched on."

items.name: Tissues
items.description: groups of cells that are similar to one another in structure and function.

items.name: Histology
items.description: study of tissues.

items.name: Four Major Types of Tissue
items.description: epithelial, connective, muscular, nervous.

items.name: Golden Exam Points (from slide)
items.description: Epithelial tissue → no blood supply · Cardiac muscle → involuntary & striated · Nervous tissue → poor regeneration

items.name: Where Found
items.description: covers the body's outer surface; lines most inner cavities (mouth, respiratory tract, reproductive tract); forms glands.

items.name: Functions
items.description: protection, absorption, filtration, secretion, transportation. e.g., epithelial tissue in the intestines absorbs water and nutrients; forms glands that secrete hormones and enzymes

items.name: What It Is Like
items.description: forms continuous sheets, like floor tiles; outer surface unattached; undersurface attached to basement membrane.

items.name: Avascular
items.description: no blood supply; depends on underlying connective tissue for nourishment. High regenerative capacity · cells tightly packed, little intercellular matrix

items.name: Simple Squamous
items.description: thin, flat cells (e.g., alveoli / air sacs in lungs).

items.name: Simple Cuboidal
items.description: in ducts and secretory portions of small glands and in kidney tubules; secretes and absorbs.

items.name: Simple Columnar
items.description: absorption & secretion (e.g., intestine); also secretes mucus and enzymes. Ciliated in bronchi, uterine tubes, and uterus; nonciliated in the digestive tract and bladder

items.name: Pseudostratified Columnar
items.description: ciliated tissue lines the trachea and much of the upper respiratory tract; secretes mucus, cilia move mucus.

items.name: Stratified Squamous
items.description: lines the esophagus, mouth, and vagina; protects against abrasion.

items.name: Stratified Cuboidal
items.description: protection (e.g., sweat glands, salivary glands, and mammary glands).

items.name: Stratified Columnar
items.description: the male urethra and the ducts of some glands; secretes and protects.

items.name: Transitional
items.description: lines the bladder, urethra, and the ureters; allows the urinary organs to expand and stretch.

items.name: Glandular Epithelia
items.description: function is secretion. Exocrine glands (release secretions through pores, e.g., sweat glands) · endocrine glands (secrete hormones)

items.name: Location
items.description: in blood, under skin, in bone, around organs.

items.name: Functions
items.description: support (organs and body structures), connection (tissues and organs together), protection (protects and cushions organs), fat storage, transportation (transports substances in the blood). Key idea: connective tissue = support + connect + protect + transport

items.name: Extracellular Matrix (ECM)
items.description: connective tissue has fewer cells and more material around the cells; this material is called the ECM. Change the extracellular matrix, and you change the type of connective tissue.

items.name: Collagen Fibres
items.description: provide strength.

items.name: Elastic Fibres
items.description: allow stretching.

items.name: Ground Substance
items.description: gel-like material around the cells.

items.name: Interstitial Fluid
items.description: helps nutrients and wastes move between blood and cells.

items.name: Connective Tissue Proper
items.description: protein fibers abundant in variable ground substance; support, binding, and protection. Loose (areolar, adipose, reticular) – flexible support, binds and cushions organs · Dense fibrous (dense regular, dense irregular, elastic; e.g., tendon, dermis) – strong support, withstands stress

items.name: Cartilage
items.description: firm but flexible connective tissue with cells in lacunae (matrix: chondroitin sulfate); flexible support and shock absorption. Hyaline, fibrocartilage, elastic · e.g., nose, ear, intervertebral disc

items.name: Bone (Osseous)
items.description: hard, mineralized connective tissue (matrix: calcium phosphate); rigid support, protection, mineral storage. Consume enough calcium

items.name: Blood and Lymph
items.description: blood is a fluid connective tissue (liquid matrix: plasma); transport, defense, and clotting. Red blood cells (erythrocytes) · white blood cells (leukocytes) · platelets (thrombocytes) · plasma

items.name: Nervous Tissue
items.description: makes up the brain, spinal cord, and nerves. Functions: communication, coordination, sensory reception

items.name: Neurons
items.description: receive and transmit impulses. Parts: dendrites, cell body, axon

items.name: Neuroglia (Glia)
items.description: assist the propagation of the nerve impulse and provide nutrients to the neurons.

items.name: Muscle Tissue
items.description: composed of cells (fibers) that contract to cause movement of a body part. Functions: locomotion, organ movement, heartbeat

items.name: Skeletal Muscle
items.description: voluntary.

items.name: Smooth Muscle
items.description: involuntary (e.g., walls of the digestive organs).

items.name: Cardiac Muscle
items.description: heart; involuntary and striated.

items.name: Phases of Tissue Repair
items.description: (1) Hemostasis → (2) Inflammation → (3) Proliferation → (4) Remodeling

items.name: Steps in Tissue Repair
items.description: Wound → clot and scab → tissue repair begins → scar tissue forms → epithelial cells multiply → scab detaches

items.name: Membranes
items.description: thin sheets of tissue that cover surfaces, line body cavities, surround organs, and lubricate different parts of the body.

items.name: Mucous Membranes
items.description: line all body cavities that open to the exterior of the body; coated with secretions of mucous glands. Respiratory, digestive, urinary, reproductive tracts

items.name: Serous Membranes
items.description: line ventral body cavities that do not open to the exterior. Pleura (parietal and visceral) · pericardium · peritoneum (parietal and visceral)

items.name: Cutaneous Membrane
items.description: the skin; covers the body surface.

items.name: Synovial Membranes
items.description: line joint cavities and produce the fluid within the joint.

items.name: Integumentary System (Skin)
items.description: largest organ of the human body; approximately 16% of human body weight; complex structure composed of various tissues. Accessories: hair, nails, oil and sweat glands

items.name: Three Layers
items.description: epidermis, dermis, hypodermis; held together by connective tissue.

items.name: Epidermis
items.description: made of closely packed epithelial cells (keratinocytes); site of pigment production (melanin) and keratin (regulates skin rigidity). Epi = upon

items.name: Dermis
items.description: made of dense, irregular connective tissue that houses blood vessels, hair follicles, sweat glands, and other structures.

items.name: Hypodermis (Subcutaneous Fat)
items.description: composed mainly of loose connective and fatty tissues. Hypo = below

items.name: Protection
items.description: forms a barrier against injury, pathogens, and water loss.

items.name: Sensory
items.description: contains receptors for touch, pressure, pain, and temperature.

items.name: Thermoregulation
items.description: helps control body temperature through sweating and blood vessel changes.

items.name: Fluid and Electrolyte Balance
items.description: helps reduce excessive fluid loss and supports balance.

items.name: Excretion
items.description: removes small amounts of water, salts, and wastes through sweat.

items.name: Elimination
items.description: contributes to removal of minor waste products through the skin.

items.name: Secretion
items.description: sebaceous glands release sebum to lubricate skin and hair.

items.name: Absorption
items.description: limited absorption of certain medications and chemicals through the skin.

items.name: Immunity
items.description: immune cells in the skin help detect and fight pathogens.

items.name: Insulation
items.description: subcutaneous tissue helps conserve body heat.

items.name: Hormone Production
items.description: UV exposure helps the skin produce vitamin D needed for calcium balance.

items.name: Stratum Corneum
items.description: outermost layer; 15–30 layers of dead, keratinized cells; protects against friction, pathogens, and water loss. Cells are continuously shed and replaced.

items.name: Stratum Lucidum
items.description: found only in thick skin, such as the palms and soles; flattened, dead keratinocytes; extra protection and durability.

items.name: Stratum Granulosum
items.description: 3–5 layers of keratinocytes that begin to flatten, die, and fill with keratin; helps form the skin's water barrier (prevents fluid loss). Corneum + lucidum + granulosum create a strong, protective, water-resistant surface.

items.name: Stratum Spinosum
items.description: 8–10 layers of keratinocytes connected by desmosomes ("spiny" appearance); keratin production begins to increase. Key function: provides strength and immune protection to the epidermis

items.name: Stratum Basale (Germinativum)
items.description: deepest layer of the epidermis; a single row of rapidly dividing basal cells that act as stem cells, producing new keratinocytes. Hemidesmosomes anchor the cells to the basal lamina.

items.name: Keratinocytes
items.description: closely packed epithelial cells of the epidermis that produce keratin.

items.name: Melanocytes
items.description: about 10–25% of cells in the stratum basale; produce melanin, which contributes to skin colour and helps protect against UV radiation.

items.name: Merkel Cells
items.description: specialized touch receptors found mainly in hairless skin (stratum basale); respond to light pressure and stimulate sensory nerve endings.

items.name: Dendritic Cells (Langerhans Cells)
items.description: immune cells in the stratum spinosum; detect and help destroy pathogens and abnormal cells.

items.name: Desmosomes
items.description: connect keratinocytes, giving the "spiny" appearance and strength to the epidermis.

items.name: Dermis
items.description: supports the epidermis; lies between the epidermis and hypodermis. Key function: provides strength, flexibility, nourishment, sensation, and support

items.name: Papillary Layer
items.description: superficial dermal layer; areolar connective tissue; contains capillaries and sensory nerve endings; nourishes the epidermis and supports touch. Dermal papillae help anchor the epidermis.

items.name: Reticular Layer
items.description: deeper, thicker dermal layer; dense irregular connective tissue; contains blood vessels, receptors, hair follicles, and glands. Collagen = strength; elastic fibers = flexibility · supports protection and temperature regulation

items.name: Hypodermis
items.description: lies beneath the dermis and connects the skin to deeper tissues; anchors the skin while still allowing movement over muscles; contains large amounts of adipose tissue. Hypo = below or under

items.name: Insulation
items.description: helps reduce heat loss.

items.name: Cushioning
items.description: protects underlying tissues from impact.

items.name: Energy Storage
items.description: stores fat as an energy reserve.

items.name: Skin Pigmentation
items.description: coloration depends on the amount of melanin produced by melanocytes in the stratum basale and taken up by keratinocytes.

items.name: Genetics
items.description: determines baseline skin colour.

items.name: UV Exposure
items.description: increases melanin production, causing tanning.

items.name: Melanin
items.description: brown-black pigment made by melanocytes in the stratum basale.

items.name: Carotene
items.description: yellow-orange pigment that accumulates in the epidermis and adipose tissue. Found in orange and yellow vegetables (e.g., carrots, sweet potatoes, squash)

items.name: Albinism
items.description: inherited condition with reduced or absent melanin production.

items.name: Key Point
items.description: differences in skin colour are mainly due to how much melanin is produced and distributed, not the number of melanocytes.

items.name: Hair
items.description: a keratin filament from the epidermis, primarily consisting of dead cells; protection and sensation. Grows from the hair follicle, penetrating the epidermis into the dermis

items.name: Hair Shaft
items.description: visible part of the hair.

items.name: Hair Root
items.description: anchored portion below; ends at the hair bulb deep in the dermis.

items.name: Hair Bulb
items.description: contains actively dividing cells; surrounds the hair papilla.

items.name: Hair Papilla
items.description: has blood vessels and nerve endings from the dermis.

items.name: Arrector Pili Muscle
items.description: causes goosebumps (piloerection).

items.name: Nails
items.description: protect the tips of fingers and toes; nail body consists of dense, dead keratinocytes.

items.name: Nail Bed
items.description: specialized part of the epidermis at fingertips and toes; forms the foundation for the nail body, protecting high stress areas. Pink appearance due to its rich blood supply

items.name: Nail Root
items.description: where nail growth occurs, with a matrix of basal cells allowing continuous growth.

items.name: Nail Cuticle (Eponychium)
items.description: forms where the nail fold meets the proximal nail body.

items.name: Lunula
items.description: visible part of the nail root.

groups.name: Accessory Structures: Glands of the Skin

items.name: Sweat Glands (Sudoriferous Glands)
items.description: produce sweat to help regulate body temperature (cooling); also help remove small amounts of waste products.

items.name: Eccrine Sweat Glands
items.description: main function is thermoregulation (body cooling); most numerous (2–4 million); open directly onto the skin surface (sweat pores). Throughout the body, especially forehead, palms, soles · sweat is mostly water and salt (NaCl), with antibodies, metabolic waste traces, and the antimicrobial peptide dermcidin · generally odorless

items.name: Apocrine Sweat Glands
items.description: scent/odor production; larger and fewer; open into hair follicles; found in densely hairy areas (armpits, genital regions, areola). Thicker sweat (proteins, lipids, organic compounds) · bacterial breakdown causes body odor

items.name: Sebaceous Glands
items.description: type of oil gland found all over body; help to lubricate and waterproof skin and hair; most are associated with hair follicles.

items.name: Sebum
items.description: a mixture of lipids made by sebaceous glands; its fatty acids have antibacterial properties and prevent water loss from skin. Sebum is stimulated by hormones.

items.name: Wound Healing
items.description: after a superficial abrasion, basal cells rapidly divide to produce new keratinocytes and repair the epidermis. If the stratum basale remains intact, the skin can heal well; if destroyed, healing is slower and may lead to scarring.

items.name: Basal Cell Carcinoma
items.description: common skin cancer that begins from cells associated with the stratum basale, often after long-term UV exposure.

items.name: Vitiligo
items.description: melanocytes are lost or destroyed, producing areas of depigmented skin.

items.name: Melanoma
items.description: melanocytes become cancerous.

items.name: Viral Warts (HPV)
items.description: human papillomavirus infects keratinocytes in the upper epidermis, causing increased cell growth and wart formation.

items.name: Dry Skin
items.description: when the stratum granulosum and corneum are impaired, water is lost more easily (e.g., eczema, dermatitis).

items.name: Blisters
items.description: separation near the dermal-epidermal junction causes fluid-filled blisters (e.g., from friction, burns).

items.name: Second-Degree Burns
items.description: damage the epidermis and extend into the dermis, causing pain, redness, swelling, and blistering.

items.name: Intradermal Injection
items.description: medication is injected into the dermis (e.g., TB or allergy testing).

items.name: Hypodermic Needle
items.description: injects into the hypodermis; subcutaneous fat, muscle and veins are all hypodermic.

items.name: Pressure Injury
items.description: prolonged pressure reduces blood flow to the dermis, damaging skin and underlying tissue.

items.name: Scar Formation
items.description: injury to the deeper reticular dermis stimulates collagen production and leads to scar tissue.

items.name: Stretch Marks (Striae)
items.description: damage and stretching of collagen and elastic fibers in the dermis.

items.name: Tattooing
items.description: pigment is placed into the dermis, which is why it remains visible long term.

items.name: Acne
items.description: disorder of the sebaceous glands and hair follicles, involving excess sebum production, clogged pores, bacterial growth, and inflammation.

modules.title: Module 3 · Blood, Body Fluid and Electrolytes
modules.course: PN Structure and Function of the Human Body · NRSG-10159
modules.topics: Blood · Formed Elements · Hemostasis · Blood Types · Body Fluids · Electrolytes · Acid–Base Balance

items.name: Cardiovascular System
items.description: fluid – blood; conducting tubes – blood vessels (capillaries, arteries, veins); pump – heart. Blood is the medium of transport: it delivers nutrients to and removes wastes from our trillions of cells.

items.name: Blood Volume
items.description: 5–6 liters in average male; 4–5 liters in average female.

items.name: Parts of Blood
items.description: cellular elements (RBCs, WBCs, platelets) + extracellular matrix: plasma (mostly water).

items.name: Blood in a Test Tube
items.description: plasma about 55% (water, proteins, nutrients, hormones) · buffy coat less than 1% (white blood cells, platelets) · red blood cells about 45%.

items.name: Hematocrit
items.description: measures the percentage of RBCs (erythrocytes) in a blood sample. Normal: female 37–47%, male 42–52% · depressed in anemia · elevated in polycythemia

items.name: Colour
items.description: oxygenated blood is bright red; deoxygenated blood is a darker red. Hemoglobin is a pigment that changes color depending on the degree of oxygen saturation.

items.name: Viscosity
items.description: blood is 5 times more viscous than water because of protein and other contents.

items.name: pH
items.description: 7.35–7.45 (more alkaline).

items.name: Temperature
items.description: 38 degrees (°C).

items.name: Transportation
items.description: transports O₂, CO₂, nutrients, hormones, wastes.

items.name: Regulation (Homeostasis)
items.description: regulates pH and ion composition by absorbing and neutralizing acids; body temperature regulation, chemical balance.

items.name: Restricting Fluid Loss
items.description: restricts fluid loss at injury sites with the clotting process.

items.name: Defense / Immunity
items.description: defends against toxins and pathogens with white blood cells and antibodies; platelets help with clotting.

items.name: Stabilizing Temperature
items.description: absorbs heat and distributes blood flow to different areas.

items.name: Plasma
items.description: 46–63% of blood; 92% water; the substances dissolved in it are mostly proteins.

items.name: Water
items.description: 92% of plasma; transport medium.

items.name: Plasma Proteins
items.description: 7% of plasma; proteins specific to plasma: albumin, globulin, fibrinogen.

items.name: Albumin
items.description: 54–60% of plasma proteins; made in the liver; maintains osmotic concentration, transports lipid molecules.

items.name: Globulins
items.description: 35–38% of plasma proteins. Alpha and beta globulins (liver) – transport, maintain osmotic concentration · gamma globulins (immunoglobulins, made by plasma cells) – immune responses

items.name: Fibrinogen
items.description: 4–7% of plasma proteins; made in the liver; blood clotting in hemostasis.

items.name: Regulatory Proteins
items.description: less than 1%; hormones and enzymes; regulate various body functions.

items.name: Other Solutes
items.description: 1%; nutrients, gases, and wastes.

items.name: Formed Elements
items.description: 37–54% of blood: erythrocytes (99%), leukocytes (less than 1%), platelets (less than 1%).

items.name: Lifespan of Formed Elements
items.description: very brief, a few hours to a few days, so the body must continuously create new blood cells.

items.name: Hemopoiesis / Hematopoiesis
items.description: the process of forming and replacing blood cells (haima- = "blood"; -poiesis = "production"). Hematopoiesis and hemopoiesis are the same process, no difference in meaning.

items.name: Red Bone Marrow
items.description: all formed elements arise from stem cells of the red bone marrow; it produces different cells at different rates. Skull, pelvis, ribs, sternum, humerus, femur

items.name: Extramedullary Hemopoiesis
items.description: when disease impairs the bone marrow, hemopoiesis begins in the liver and spleen, causing the spleen to enlarge.

items.name: Hematopoietic Stem Cell (Hemocytoblast)
items.description: multipotent stem cell that becomes a myeloid or lymphoid stem cell. Myeloid → platelets (megakaryocyte), erythrocyte, basophil, neutrophil, eosinophil, monocyte (macrophage) · Lymphoid → natural killer cell, T lymphocyte, B lymphocyte (plasma cell)

items.name: Hemopoietic Growth Factors
items.description: stimulate blood cell formation.

items.name: Erythropoietin (EPO)
items.description: stimulates RBCs; secreted by the kidneys.

items.name: Thrombopoietin
items.description: stimulates platelets; secreted by the liver and kidneys.

items.name: Cytokines
items.description: stimulate defense cells; made by different cells.

items.name: Erythrocytes
items.description: mature in the red bone marrow; transport blood gases, primarily oxygen and some carbon dioxide. RBCs make up about 1/3 of all cells in the human body.

items.name: Shape
items.description: biconcave discs with very shallow centers; optimizes surface area to volume for gas exchange and lets them fold up in narrow blood vessels.

items.name: Hemoglobin
items.description: iron-containing protein that binds with oxygen. One erythrocyte can contain 300 million hemoglobin molecules, so more than 1 billion oxygen molecules.

items.name: Erythropoiesis
items.description: production of red blood cells; stimulated by EPO from the kidneys. Check with teacher: the slide says erythropoiesis is "stimulated by an increase in the CO₂ level in the blood." Most textbooks teach that low oxygen (hypoxia) makes the kidneys release EPO.

items.name: Production Needs
items.description: glucose, lipids, and amino acids, plus iron, copper, zinc, and B vitamins.

items.name: Life Span
items.description: up to 120 days; worn-out cells are removed by macrophages.

items.name: RBC Breakdown
items.description: iron is reabsorbed by the body; bilirubin is absorbed by the liver and helps form bile, giving it its yellow color. Bile emulsifies fat and gives feces its brown color · bilirubin can also be removed from blood into urine

items.name: Anemia
items.description: ineffective hematopoiesis results in insufficient numbers of RBCs; with insufficient hemoglobin, tissues may not receive enough oxygen (hypoxemia). Depressed hematocrit

items.name: Anemias from Faulty or Decreased RBC Production
items.description: sickle cell anemia, iron deficiency anemia, vitamin deficiency anemia, and diseases of the bone marrow and stem cells.

items.name: Sickle Cell Anemia
items.description: caused by a mutation in one of the hemoglobin genes; abnormal hemoglobin makes the cell take on a sickle or crescent shape.

items.name: Thalassemia
items.description: genetic disorder with abnormal synthesis of globin proteins and excessive destruction of erythrocytes; patients are usually jaundiced with excessive bilirubin.

items.name: Jaundice
items.description: yellowish discoloration of the skin, mucous membranes, and whites of the eyes (sclera), caused by elevated bilirubin in the blood (hyperbilirubinemia).

items.name: Polycythemia
items.description: overproduction of RBCs; the main drawback is increased viscosity of the blood, which makes it harder for the heart to circulate blood. Elevated hematocrit · polycythemia vera: bone marrow overproduces red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets

items.name: Leukocytes
items.description: a major component of the body's defenses against disease; defend against pathogens (bacteria, viruses, parasites, tumors). Can move between blood and tissues · far less numerous, larger, and shorter life span than erythrocytes

items.name: Emigration (Diapedesis)
items.description: leukocytes leave the blood by squeezing through adjacent cells in a blood vessel wall. They follow chemical signals to the site of injury or infection.

items.name: Granular Leukocytes
items.description: neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils; nonspecific immunity.

items.name: Neutrophils
items.description: most commonly found; rapid responders; small in size; perform phagocytosis during an acute infection.

items.name: Eosinophils
items.description: antihistamine feature; allergic and parasitic reactions.

items.name: Basophils
items.description: least common; intensify inflammation. Release heparin (an anticoagulant)

items.name: Agranular Leukocytes
items.description: lymphocytes and monocytes.

items.name: Lymphocytes
items.description: natural killer cells, B cells, and T cells; specific immunity.

items.name: Natural Killer Cells
items.description: non-specific immunity; large cell; cytotoxic traits.

items.name: B Cells
items.description: acquired immunity; produce plasma cells that produce plasma proteins (antibodies).

items.name: T Cells
items.description: acquired immunity; cell-mediated response.

items.name: Monocytes
items.description: largest leukocyte; become macrophages; nonspecific immunity.

items.name: Macrophages
items.description: phagocytic cells; high numbers in lymph nodes.

items.name: Leukopenia
items.description: too few leukocytes are produced; if pronounced, the person may be unable to ward off disease. Most important nursing action shown on the slide: hand washing (infection prevention)

items.name: Leukocytosis
items.description: excessive leukocyte proliferation.

items.name: Leukemia
items.description: cancer involving an abundance of leukocytes; may involve one type from the myeloid line (myelocytic leukemia) or the lymphoid line (lymphocytic leukemia).

items.name: Lymphoma
items.description: cancer in which masses of malignant T and/or B lymphocytes collect in lymph nodes, the spleen, the liver, and other tissues; the patient is vulnerable to infection. Some forms progress slowly and respond well to treatment; others progress quickly and need aggressive treatment.

items.name: Platelets
items.description: not actually cells, just fragments of cells (from megakaryocytes); needed for the clotting process. Life span of about 9–12 days

items.name: Platelet Count
items.description: low number means more bleeding; high number means clotting.

items.name: Functions
items.description: essential for repairing damaged blood vessels; provide growth factors for healing and repair; cling to broken vessels or tissues to help control blood loss.

items.name: Thrombocytopenia
items.description: insufficient number of platelets; blood may not clot properly, and excessive bleeding may result.

items.name: Thrombocytosis
items.description: too many platelets; may trigger formation of unwanted blood clots (thrombosis), a potentially fatal disorder.

items.name: 1. Vascular Spasm (Vessel Constriction)
items.description: smooth muscle in the walls of the vessel contracts dramatically.

items.name: 2. Platelet Plug (Primary Hemostasis)
items.description: platelets clump together, become spiked and sticky, and bind to the exposed collagen and endothelial lining.

items.name: 3. Coagulation (Fibrin Clot Conversion)
items.description: more durable repairs made beyond the plug; the formation of a blood clot.

items.name: Venospasm (IV Insertion)
items.description: contraction of the vein as a protective mechanism; a consideration for both insertion and removal of IVs. Hold the site for a few moments after removal while a platelet plug forms.

items.name: Intrinsic Pathway
items.description: factors XII, XI, IX, VIII; measured by aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time).

items.name: Extrinsic Pathway
items.description: tissue factor and factor VII; measured by PT (prothrombin time).

items.name: Common Pathway
items.description: factor X (with factor V, Ca++ and lipids) turns prothrombin (II) into thrombin; thrombin turns fibrinogen (I) into a fibrin clot (XIII).

items.name: Components Needed for Clotting
items.description: platelets, clotting factors, calcium (Ca++), lipids, prothrombin, fibrinogen.

items.name: Anticoagulant (Blood Thinner)
items.description: any substance that opposes coagulation; slows the blood from clotting too quickly. Plasma anticoagulants limit clotting to the region of injury and restore a normal, clot-free condition of blood.

items.name: Protein C System
items.description: inactivates clotting factors involved in the intrinsic pathway.

items.name: TFPI (Tissue Factor Pathway Inhibitor)
items.description: inhibits the conversion of inactive factor VII to the active form in the extrinsic pathway.

items.name: Antithrombin
items.description: inactivates factor X and opposes the conversion of prothrombin (factor II) to thrombin in the common pathway.

items.name: Heparin
items.description: short-acting anticoagulant released by basophils that also opposes prothrombin; also found on cells lining the blood vessels. A pharmaceutical form is given to surgical patients at risk for blood clots.

items.name: Fibrinolysis
items.description: the gradual degradation of the clot, to restore normal blood flow as the vessel heals.

items.name: Plasmin
items.description: the active form of plasminogen; gradually breaks down the fibrin of the clot.

items.name: Bradykinin
items.description: a vasodilator that reverses the effects of serotonin and prostaglandins from platelets, letting vessel smooth muscle relax and restoring circulation.

items.name: Platelet Production
items.description: either an insufficient or an excessive production of platelets can lead to severe disease or death.

items.name: Hemophilia
items.description: genetic disorder of inadequate production of functional amounts of one or more clotting factors. Patients bleed from even minor wounds and leak blood into joint spaces after exercise and into urine and stool.

items.name: Thrombus (plural: thrombi)
items.description: a blood clot that forms in a blood vessel; platelets, erythrocytes and WBCs trapped within a mass of fibrin strands. Can form in an intact or only slightly damaged vessel · impedes blood flow and raises local blood pressure, so the heart must pump harder

items.name: Thrombosis
items.description: a condition characterized by excessive numbers of platelets that increases the risk for excessive clot formation.

items.name: Thrombophilia (Hypercoagulation)
items.description: a tendency to form thrombosis; may be familial (genetic) or acquired. Acquired: lupus, immune reactions to heparin, polycythemia vera, thrombocytosis, sickle cell disease, pregnancy, obesity

items.name: Venous Stasis
items.description: blood in the veins, particularly in the legs, remains stationary for long periods.

items.name: DVT (Deep Vein Thrombosis)
items.description: a blood clot forms in a deep vein (back of the knee/calf); due to immobilization or after surgery; dangerous if a piece breaks off and travels to the heart/lungs. Signs: calf swelling, erythema (redness), and leg warmth

items.name: Embolus
items.description: a portion of a thrombus that breaks free from the vessel wall and enters the circulation ("on the move!").

items.name: Blood Groups
items.description: determined by the presence or absence of specific marker molecules on the plasma membranes of erythrocytes.

items.name: Antigens
items.description: substances the body does not recognize as "self", which trigger a defensive response from the leukocytes.

items.name: ABO Blood Group
items.description: designates the presence or absence of just two antigens (A and B). Normally the body must be exposed to an antigen before making antibodies, but ABO antibodies are preformed (no prior exposure needed).

items.name: Type A
items.description: A antigen; anti-B antibodies; compatible in an emergency: A, O.

items.name: Type B
items.description: B antigen; anti-A antibodies; compatible in an emergency: B, O.

items.name: Type AB
items.description: A and B antigens; no antibodies; compatible: A, B, AB, O (AB+ is the universal recipient).

items.name: Type O
items.description: no A or B antigens; anti-A and anti-B antibodies; compatible: O only (O is the universal donor).

items.name: Rh Blood Group
items.description: based on the presence or absence of a second erythrocyte antigen, Rh; Rh D antigen present = positive (+), absent = negative (–).

items.name: Homeostasis
items.description: maintenance of constant conditions in the body; substances in chemical reactions must stay within narrow ranges of concentration. Too much or too little of a single substance can disrupt bodily functions · water is the most common substance in the chemical reactions of life

items.name: Fluid Compartment
items.description: a location largely separate from another compartment by some form of physical barrier.

items.name: Intracellular Fluid (ICF)
items.description: all fluid enclosed in cells by their plasma membranes; the principal component of the cytosol/cytoplasm. About 60% of total body water (about 25 L in an average adult male) – the largest compartment

items.name: Extracellular Fluid (ECF)
items.description: surrounds all cells in the body; made of plasma and interstitial fluid.

items.name: Interstitial Fluid (IF)
items.description: surrounds all cells not in the blood; second largest volume. Materials travel between cells and the plasma in capillaries through the IF.

items.name: Plasma (ECF)
items.description: the fluid component of the blood.

items.name: Fluid Intake (2600–3000 mL total)
items.description: ingested water 1200–1500 mL · ingested food 800–1100 mL · metabolic oxidation 300 mL

items.name: Fluid Output (2600–3000 mL total)
items.description: kidneys 1500 mL · insensible loss through skin 600–800 mL · insensible loss through lungs 400–600 mL · GI tract 100 mL

items.name: Sodium (Na+)
items.description: 135 to 145 mmol/L

items.name: Potassium (K+)
items.description: 3.5 to 5.0 mmol/L

items.name: Bicarbonate (HCO₃)
items.description: 21 to 28 mmol/L

items.name: Magnesium (Mg)
items.description: 0.65 to 1.05 mmol/L

items.name: Phosphorus (P)
items.description: 0.97 to 1.45 mmol/L

items.name: Electrolyte Imbalances
items.description: hypo-/hyper- natremia (sodium) · kalemia (potassium) · calcemia (calcium) · magnesemia (magnesium) · chloremia (chloride) · phosphatemia (phosphate)

items.name: Sodium
items.description: extracellular ion; regulates water movement (osmosis) across the cell membrane, as water moves from lower sodium concentration to higher concentration.

items.name: Hyponatremia
items.description: low blood sodium (below 135). Mnemonic on slide, SALT LOSS: stupor/coma · anorexia (nausea & vomiting) · lethargy · tendon reflex · limp muscle (weakness) · orthostatic hypotension · seizures/headache · stomach cramping Check with teacher: the slide says "sodium less than 145 mEq/L" and lists water deprivation, thirst, and dry sticky mucous membranes. Those signs match hypernatremia, and since normal is 135–145, hyponatremia should be below 135.

items.name: Hypernatremia
items.description: abnormal increase in blood sodium; can result from water loss from the blood (hemoconcentration). Symptoms: neuromuscular irritability, convulsions, CNS lethargy, coma · hormonal imbalances (ADH, aldosterone) raise sodium · Causes, MODEL: medications/meals (too much sodium), osmotic diuretics, diabetes insipidus, excessive water loss, low water intake

items.name: Potassium (K+)
items.description: major intracellular ion; helps establish the resting membrane potential in neurons and muscle fibres. Little effect on osmotic pressure · excreted actively and passively through the kidney (renal tubules)

items.name: Hyperkalemia
items.description: elevated K+ blood level, above 5.5 mEq/L. Causes: increased dietary intake; K+ entering the ECF in high concentrations · Symptoms: impairs skeletal muscle, nervous system, and heart; mental confusion, numbness, weakened respiratory muscles Check with teacher: the normal range slide says 3.5–5.0, but this slide uses "above 5.5." Ask which cut-off the exam uses.

items.name: Hypokalemia
items.description: K+ below 3.5 mEq/L. Causes: reduced K+ in the body or blood (redistribution), decreased intake (starvation), vomiting, diarrhea, alkalosis · Symptoms: alkalosis, ECG changes, cardiac arrhythmias, muscle weakness, paresthesia, leg cramps, fatigue, lethargy, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, decreased bowel sounds and motility

items.name: Calcium
items.description: most plentiful electrolyte in the body; used to form bones; mainly absorbed and excreted through the GI system. Mostly extracellular; crucial for neurons, muscle cells, enzymes, and coagulation · regulated by the parathyroid gland with parathyroid hormone (PTH)

items.name: Magnesium
items.description: mostly found in the bones and within cells; important in control of metabolism and numerous enzyme reactions.

items.name: Hypermagnesemia
items.description: serum magnesium above 2.5 mg/dL. Causes: abnormal kidney function, antacids or laxatives with magnesium · Symptoms: mild – nausea, flushing, tiredness; decreased deep tendon reflexes; severe – paralysis, respiratory failure, bradycardia → cardiac arrest · Treatment: stop the magnesium source (if kidneys normal), diuretic, dialysis

items.name: Hypomagnesemia
items.description: low serum magnesium. Causes: GI losses (vomiting, diarrhea), diuretics, alcohol use, hypercalcemia, genetic disorders, low dietary intake · Symptoms: usually with other electrolyte imbalances; severe – arrhythmias, seizures, tetany · Treatment: magnesium orally or IV; treat other deficiencies

items.name: pH
items.description: low pH = acidic (high H+); high pH = alkaline (low H+); 7 = neutral.

items.name: Normal Body pH
items.description: 7.35–7.45. Acidosis below 7.35 · alkalosis above 7.45 · death below 6.8 or above 7.8

items.name: Regulated By
items.description: buffers, respiratory system, renal system.

items.name: Factors Affecting Fluid, Electrolyte and Acid–Base Balance
items.description: age, gender, body size, environmental temperature, lifestyle, chronic diseases, acute conditions, medications, treatments, extremes of age, inability to access food and fluids.

modules.title: Module 4 · Cardiovascular System
modules.course: PN Structure and Function of the Human Body · NRSG-10159
modules.topics: The Heart (Chapter 19) · Conduction · Cardiac Cycle · Cardiac Output · Blood Vessels · Blood Pressure · Pulses

items.name: Location
items.description: mediastinum within the thoracic cavity, between the lungs; within the pericardial sac.

items.name: Orientation
items.description: dorsal surface near vertebrae; anterior surface deep to sternum and costal cartilages; great veins and arteries attached to the superior surface (base). Right side deflects forward, left side deflects backward.

items.name: Base of the Heart
items.description: level of the third costal cartilage.

items.name: Apex of the Heart
items.description: positioned just left of the sternum, between the fourth and fifth ribs. Apex's leftward deviation creates a cardiac notch in the left lung.

items.name: Clinical Relevance
items.description: location is important for stethoscope placement and imaging.

items.name: Heart Shape
items.description: inverted pear, wider at the top, narrowing toward the apex.

items.name: Average Size
items.description: length 12 cm (5 in), width 8 cm (3.5 in), thickness 6 cm (2.5 in); about the size of your fist.

items.name: Sex Difference
items.description: female heart 250–300 grams (9 to 11 oz); male heart 300–350 grams (11 to 12 oz).

items.name: Exercise Adaptation
items.description: athletes' hearts can enlarge due to exercise-induced hypertrophy.

items.name: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
items.description: can cause dangerous heart enlargement and sudden death in apparently healthy young individuals.

items.name: Epicardium
items.description: outermost layer, also known as the visceral pericardium; composed of a mesothelium reinforced with connective tissue; secretes serous fluid that lubricates the pericardial cavity.

items.name: Myocardium
items.description: middle and thickest layer, primarily composed of cardiac muscle cells; responsible for heart contractions, pumping blood into major arteries. Supported by collagenous fibers, blood vessels, and nerve fibers

items.name: Endocardium
items.description: deepest layer lining the heart's chambers, consisting of endothelial tissue.

items.name: Pericardium
items.description: surrounds the heart and the roots of the major vessels, forming the pericardial cavity; fibrous (protective) and serous (inner) layers.

items.name: Pericardial Sac
items.description: two fused layers: outer fibrous capsule and inner parietal pericardium with a serous membrane. Serous pericardium = parietal pericardium + visceral pericardium

items.name: Pericardial Cavity
items.description: filled with lubricating serous fluid, reducing friction during heart contractions.

items.name: Atria
items.description: receiving chambers (right atrium, left atrium).

items.name: Ventricles
items.description: discharging chambers (right ventricle, left ventricle); pump blood into vessels.

items.name: Right Atrium
items.description: receives blood from vena cava and coronary sinus; maintains constant blood flow.

items.name: Right Ventricle
items.description: receives blood via tricuspid valve; pushes blood to the pulmonary trunk.

items.name: Left Atrium
items.description: gets oxygen-rich blood from pulmonary veins; serves as a receiving chamber for the left ventricle.

items.name: Left Ventricle
items.description: thicker muscle layer; pumps blood to the aorta.

items.name: Vena Cava (superior and inferior)
items.description: carries blood to the heart (right atrium).

items.name: Pulmonary Artery
items.description: carries blood away from the heart to the lungs.

items.name: Pulmonary Veins
items.description: return blood from the lungs to the heart (left atrium).

items.name: Aorta
items.description: carries blood to the body.

items.name: Pulmonary Circuit
items.description: sends blood to the lungs for oxygenation.

items.name: Systemic Circuit
items.description: distributes oxygenated blood to body tissues.

items.name: Dual Pump
items.description: the heart operates in both circuits; atria receive and ventricles pump blood.

items.name: Blood Flow
items.description: right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to lungs → oxygenated blood returns to the left atrium → left ventricle sends oxygenated blood into the body.

items.name: Return to Heart
items.description: deoxygenated blood from body tissues returns through veins to superior and inferior vena cavae, then back to the right atrium.

items.name: Vessel Order
items.description: arteries → arterioles → capillaries → venules → veins → back to the heart.

items.name: Tricuspid Valve (Right AV Valve)
items.description: between the right atrium and right ventricle; three leaflets of endocardium; prevents backflow from right ventricle to right atrium. Connected to papillary muscles by chordae tendineae, which control opening and closing

items.name: Pulmonary Valve (Pulmonary Semilunar Valve)
items.description: at the base of the pulmonary trunk; three flaps; prevents backflow from the pulmonary trunk into the right ventricle. No chordae tendineae or papillary muscles; blood filling the flaps causes closure

items.name: Mitral Valve (Bicuspid, Left AV Valve)
items.description: between the left atrium and left ventricle; two cusps; prevents backflow from left ventricle to left atrium. Cusps connected to papillary muscles by chordae tendineae

items.name: Aortic Valve (Aortic Semilunar Valve)
items.description: at the base of the aorta; three flaps; prevents backflow from the aorta into the left ventricle. Blood filling the cusps during ventricular relaxation causes closure

items.name: Chordae Tendineae
items.description: connect AV valve cusps to papillary muscles and control the opening and closing.

items.name: Coronary Arteries
items.description: supply blood to the heart muscle; arise from the first section of the aorta, just after the left ventricle.

items.name: Left Coronary Artery (LCA)
items.description: supplies the left atrium, left ventricle, and interventricular septum; arises from the left posterior aortic sinus. Branches: circumflex artery (Cx) and anterior interventricular artery (LAD)

items.name: Right Coronary Artery (RCA)
items.description: supplies the right atrium, portions of both ventricles, and the heart's conduction system; arises from the anterior aortic sinus. Branches: marginal arteries and posterior interventricular artery (posterior descending artery)

items.name: Anastomoses
items.description: interconnecting smaller vessels that help maintain blood circulation in case of partial blockages.

items.name: Blockage Consequences
items.description: can lead to myocardial infarction (cell death) in the affected area due to limited bypass capacity.

groups.name: Clinical Connections: CPR and Cardiac Tamponade

items.name: CPR (Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation)
items.description: the heart's position in the torso allows CPR; manual chest compressions maintain blood flow.

items.name: Cardiac Tamponade
items.description: excess fluid in the pericardial space hampers heart relaxation; gradual buildup can accommodate volume or swiftly trigger tamponade. Causes: myocardial rupture, pericarditis, cancer, or post-surgery complications · untreated can be fatal

items.name: Tamponade Treatment
items.description: drainage tubes inserted to remove excess fluid. Premature tube removal or clot formation post-surgery can cause this condition.

items.name: Smaller Cells
items.description: cardiac muscle cells are generally smaller than skeletal muscle cells.

items.name: Striations
items.description: striped (striated) appearance, like skeletal muscle, due to the organized arrangement of protein filaments.

items.name: Autorhythmicity
items.description: pacemaker cells can generate action potentials spontaneously without nervous system input.

items.name: Energy Supply
items.description: many mitochondria, providing the energy needed for continuous and strong contractions.

items.name: Nuclei
items.description: single nucleus, unlike skeletal muscle cells which can have multiple nuclei.

items.name: Intercalated Discs
items.description: connect cardiac muscle cells (shown on the diagram with desmosomes and gap junctions).

items.name: Myocardial Contractile Cells
items.description: majority (99%) of cells in the atria and ventricles; responsible for heart contractions, pumping blood.

items.name: Myocardial Conducting Cells
items.description: small percentage (1%) of cells; form the heart's conduction system; initiate and propagate the electrical impulse (action potential). Function similar to neurons, despite being specialized muscle cells

items.name: Pacemaker Cells
items.description: specialized cells controlling heart rate (autorhythmicity); controlled by the autonomic nervous system (ANS) and responsive to hormones.

items.name: SA (Sinoatrial) Node
items.description: natural pacemaker of the heart (primary pacemaker); small group of specialized cells in the upper wall of the right atrium. Generates impulses that set the rhythm (60–100 beats per minute) · initiates atrial contraction · spreads the signal through the atria

items.name: AV (Atrioventricular) Node
items.description: secondary pacemaker; in the lower part of the interatrial septum, near the coronary sinus above the tricuspid valve; regulates the flow of electrical signals between the atria and ventricles. Briefly delays the impulse for effective ventricular pumping

items.name: Bundle of His
items.description: carries the impulse from the AV node to the bundle branches.

items.name: Bundle Branches (Right and Left)
items.description: together with Purkinje fibers, coordinate ventricular contractions.

items.name: Purkinje Fibers
items.description: spread the impulse through the ventricles, coordinating ventricular contraction.

items.name: Systole
items.description: contraction period when the heart pumps blood.

items.name: Diastole
items.description: relaxation period when the chambers fill with blood.

items.name: Relaxed Start
items.description: both atria and ventricles are relaxed (diastole); blood flows into the atria; AV valves open; semilunar valves closed.

items.name: Atrial Systole
items.description: following atrial depolarization (P wave), atrial muscles contract, pushing blood into the ventricles. Contributes 20–30% of ventricular filling · lasts about 100 ms

items.name: Ventricular Systole
items.description: two phases: isovolumic contraction and ventricular ejection.

items.name: Isovolumic Contraction
items.description: increases ventricular pressure, but no ejection yet.

items.name: Ventricular Ejection
items.description: pressure rises to open semilunar valves and pump blood. Stroke volume around 70–80 mL

items.name: End Systolic Volume (ESV)
items.description: approximately 50–60 mL of blood remaining in the ventricle.

items.name: Ventricular Diastole
items.description: two phases: isovolumic relaxation (early) and late diastole.

items.name: Isovolumic Relaxation
items.description: pressure drops without volume change.

items.name: Late Diastole (Ventricular Filling)
items.description: pressure drops below atrial pressure; blood flows from atria to ventricles; AV valves open and both chambers are in diastole.

items.name: Auscultation
items.description: a method used to listen to sounds of the body during a physical examination.

items.name: S1 ("lub")
items.description: closure of atrioventricular valves during ventricular contraction.

items.name: S2 ("dub")
items.description: closure of semilunar valves during ventricular diastole.

items.name: S3 ("Kentucky gallop")
items.description: occurs rarely in healthy individuals, possibly due to blood flow or tensing of chordae tendineae; indication of heart failure if heard later in life.

items.name: S4 ("Tennessee gallop")
items.description: due to atrial contraction forcing blood into a stiff or hypertrophic ventricle; indicates left ventricular failure if occurring before S1.

items.name: S3 + S4 Combined
items.description: occurs in some individuals with both S3 and S4. Check with teacher: the slide calls this "S7." There is no S7 heart sound; when S3 and S4 are both heard it is usually called a summation gallop.

items.name: Murmurs
items.description: unusual sounds due to turbulent blood flow, often caused by valve problems. Incompetent valves cause a "swish"; stiff valves give a high-pitched sound · graded on a scale of 1 to 6 · detected with phonocardiograms or auscultograms

items.name: Aortic Area
items.description: 2nd ICS (intercostal space) to the right sternal border.

items.name: Pulmonic Area
items.description: 2nd ICS to the left sternal border.

items.name: Erb's Point
items.description: 3rd ICS to the left sternal border.

items.name: Tricuspid Area
items.description: 5th ICS to the lower left sternal border.

items.name: Mitral Area
items.description: apex, PMI (point of maximum impulse) and 5th ICS at MCL (midclavicular line).

items.name: Cardiac Output (CO)
items.description: how much blood the heart pumps in one minute. CO = HR × SV

items.name: Heart Rate (HR)
items.description: how many times the heart beats in one minute; around 75 bpm with a range of 60–100.

items.name: Stroke Volume (SV)
items.description: measured using echocardiogram or specialized catheter; typically averages about 70 mL. SV = End Diastolic Volume (EDV) – End Systolic Volume (ESV) · normal range 55–100 mL

items.name: Compensation
items.description: if SV decreases, CO can be maintained by increasing HR.

items.name: Factors Affecting HR
items.description: autonomic innervation, hormones, fitness levels, age.

items.name: Factors Affecting SV
items.description: heart size, fitness levels, gender, contractility, duration of contraction, preload (EDV), afterload (resistance).

items.name: Increased Output
items.description: elevated heart rate or stroke volume; triggered by sympathetic stimulation, catecholamines, thyroid hormones, and increased calcium levels.

items.name: Reduced Output
items.description: reduced heart rate or stroke volume; influenced by parasympathetic stimulation, changes in potassium or calcium levels, anoxia, and acidosis.

groups.name: Factors Changing Heart Rate and Force of Contraction

items.name: Autonomic Nerves
items.description: Increase: cardioaccelerator nerves release norepinephrine · Decrease: cardioinhibitor nerves (vagus) release acetylcholine

items.name: Proprioreceptors
items.description: Increase: increased firing during exercise · Decrease: decreased firing following exercise

items.name: Chemoreceptors
items.description: Increase: decreased O₂; increased H+, CO₂ and lactic acid · Decrease: increased O₂; decreased H+ and CO₂

items.name: Baroreceptors
items.description: Increase: decreased firing (falling blood volume/pressure) · Decrease: increased firing (higher blood volume/pressure)

items.name: Limbic System
items.description: Increase: anticipation of physical exercise or strong emotions · Decrease: anticipation of relaxation

items.name: Catecholamines
items.description: Increase: increased epinephrine and norepinephrine · Decrease: decreased epinephrine and norepinephrine

items.name: Thyroid Hormones
items.description: Increase: increased T₃ and T₄ · Decrease: decreased T₃ and T₄

items.name: Calcium
items.description: Increase: increased Ca²⁺ · Decrease: decreased Ca²⁺

items.name: Potassium
items.description: Increase: decreased K+ · Decrease: increased K+

items.name: Sodium
items.description: Increase: decreased Na+ · Decrease: increased Na+

items.name: Body Temperature
items.description: Increase: increased body temperature · Decrease: decreased body temperature

items.name: Nicotine and Caffeine
items.description: stimulants, increasing heart rate.

items.name: Medulla Oblongata
items.description: controls heart rate via the cardiovascular centres.

items.name: Proprioreceptors
items.description: detect physical activity; increase HR for more blood flow.

items.name: Baroreceptors
items.description: sense blood pressure changes; adjust HR to maintain balance.

items.name: Chemoreceptors
items.description: monitor chemical changes (like CO₂ levels); adjust HR for proper blood flow.

items.name: Emotional Impact
items.description: stress and anxiety can increase HR; relaxation techniques (deep breathing, meditation) can lower HR.

items.name: Arteries
items.description: transport blood away from the heart; thick walls (round in cross-section); branch into arterioles.

items.name: Arterioles
items.description: distribute blood to capillary beds where exchange with body tissues occurs.

items.name: Capillaries
items.description: microscopic vessels where exchange of nutrients and wastes occurs; connect to venules.

items.name: Venules
items.description: continuous with the post-capillary venules; move blood away from the capillary beds; many venules unite to form a vein.

items.name: Veins
items.description: return deoxygenated blood from the capillaries to the heart (except the pulmonary veins).

items.name: Arterial System
items.description: high-pressure, thick-walled arteries; smaller lumens maintain blood pressure.

items.name: Venous System
items.description: low-pressure, larger-lumen veins with thinner walls; valves (especially in limb veins) aid blood flow towards the heart.

items.name: Tunica Intima
items.description: innermost layer of the vessel wall.

items.name: Tunica Media
items.description: middle layer containing smooth muscle and elastic fibers.

items.name: Tunica Externa
items.description: outermost layer providing structural support.

items.name: Systemic Circuit (vessels)
items.description: arteries supply oxygen-rich blood to body tissues; veins return blood with less oxygen.

items.name: Pulmonary Circuit (vessels)
items.description: arteries carry blood low in oxygen to the lungs; pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood to the heart.

items.name: Direction of Blood Flow
items.description: Arteries: away from the heart · Veins: toward the heart

items.name: General Appearance
items.description: Arteries: rounded · Veins: irregular, often collapsed

items.name: Pressure
items.description: Arteries: high · Veins: low

items.name: Wall Thickness
items.description: Arteries: thick · Veins: thin

items.name: Relative Oxygen Concentration
items.description: Arteries: higher in systemic arteries, lower in pulmonary arteries · Veins: lower in systemic veins, higher in pulmonary veins

items.name: Valves
items.description: Arteries: not present · Veins: present most commonly in limbs and in veins inferior to the heart

items.name: Initiation
items.description: blood flow begins with heart ventricle contractions; affected by resistance and hydrostatic pressure.

items.name: Systolic Pressure
items.description: pressure during heart contraction.

items.name: Diastolic Pressure
items.description: pressure during relaxation.

items.name: Pulse Pressure
items.description: the difference between systolic and diastolic pressures, typically at least 25% of systolic pressure.

items.name: Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP)
items.description: average pressure in arteries; MAP ≈ diastolic BP + (systolic BP – diastolic BP) / 3.

items.name: Sphygmomanometer Technique
items.description: developed by Dr. Nikolai Korotkoff; cuff wrapped around the arm at heart level, inflated to halt blood flow, then air slowly released while listening at the anterior elbow.

items.name: Korotkoff Sounds
items.description: five recognized sounds, but typically only two are recorded. First sound heard = systolic pressure · sounds disappear when the vessel fully opens = diastolic pressure

items.name: Compliance
items.description: the capacity of vessels to expand and accommodate blood. Better compliance reduces resistance and pressure · stiffened arteries increase resistance, turbulence, pressure, and the heart's workload

items.name: Viscosity
items.description: higher viscosity increases resistance and reduces flow (hematocrit).

items.name: Vessel Length
items.description: longer vessels increase resistance; shorter ones reduce resistance.

items.name: Vessel Diameter
items.description: vasoconstriction or vasodilation significantly alters resistance and flow. Narrower vessel = more resistance; wider vessel = less resistance

items.name: Pulse Mechanics
items.description: arterial elastic fibers create the pulse by expanding and recoiling.

items.name: Pulse Measurement
items.description: recorded as beats per minute by lightly pressing (palpating) accessible arteries close to the body surface; indicates heart rate and health status.

items.name: Pulse Strength
items.description: reflects cardiac output; strong pulse indicates high systolic pressure.

items.name: Pulse Sites (head to foot)
items.description: temporal, facial, common carotid, brachial, radial, femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, dorsalis pedis arteries.

items.name: Common Palpation Sites
items.description: wrist (radial artery), neck (common carotid).

items.name: Neural Regulation
