items.description: brain's cardiovascular centers control cardiac and vascular functions.

items.name: Baroreceptor Reflexes
items.description: specialized receptors in blood vessels regulate blood pressure.

items.name: Chemoreceptor Reflexes
items.description: monitor oxygen, carbon dioxide and pH levels.

items.name: Endocrine Regulation
items.description: hormonal control influences heart rate, vessel tone and fluid balance.

items.name: Autoregulation of Perfusion
items.description: local mechanisms adjust blood flow based on tissue needs.

items.name: Blood Flow Redistribution
items.description: the cardiovascular system reallocates blood flow to maintain homeostasis and meet tissue metabolic needs.

items.name: During Exercise
items.description: more blood to skeletal muscles, heart and lungs; skin (integumentary) gets more blood flow to dissipate excess heat.

items.name: Post-Meal
items.description: blood directed to digestive system for nutrient absorption and digestion.

items.name: Brain
items.description: receives consistent blood supply regardless of activity.

items.name: Hypovolemic Shock
items.description: due to severe blood loss or fluid reduction. Symptoms: rapid heart rate, weak pulse, cool skin · treated with IV fluids and pressure-increasing drugs

items.name: Cardiogenic Shock
items.description: results from heart failure or heart attack; treatment focuses on repairing heart damage.

items.name: Vascular Shock
items.description: arterioles excessively dilate; treatments involve fluid replacement and medication.

items.name: Obstructive Shock
items.description: caused by vascular blockages; treatments include fluids, anticoagulants, or surgery. Causes: pulmonary embolism, valve stenosis, cardiac tamponade, or pneumothorax

groups.name: Circulatory System and Other Body Systems

items.name: Digestive
items.description: absorbs nutrients and water; delivers nutrients to the liver via the hepatic portal vein; provides nutrients for hematopoiesis and building hemoglobin.

items.name: Endocrine
items.description: delivers hormones (atrial natriuretic hormone, epinephrine, angiotensin II, ADH, thyroxine) to help regulate blood volume and pressure.

items.name: Integumentary
items.description: carries clotting factors, platelets, and WBCs; regulates temperature by controlling blood flow to the surface; acts as a blood reservoir.

items.name: Lymphatic
items.description: transports WBCs and antibodies; excess tissue fluid not reabsorbed by capillaries goes back to the lymphatic system.

items.name: Muscular
items.description: provides nutrients and oxygen for contraction; removes lactic acid; muscular pumps aid venous return.

items.name: Nervous
items.description: produces CSF within choroid plexuses; contributes to blood–brain barrier; cardiac and vasomotor centers regulate cardiac output and blood flow.

items.name: Reproductive
items.description: aids in erection of genitalia; transports gonadotropic hormones.

items.name: Respiratory
items.description: provides blood for exchange of gases (oxygen in, carbon dioxide out).

items.name: Skeletal
items.description: provides calcium, phosphate and minerals for bone matrix; transports hormones; erythropoietin stimulates myeloid cell hematopoiesis.

items.name: Urinary
items.description: delivers 20% of resting circulation to kidneys for filtering; regulates blood volume and pressure; renin for the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone mechanism.

items.name: Aorta
items.description: the largest artery in the body; originates from the left ventricle; bifurcates into the common iliac arteries at the 4th lumbar vertebra. Distributes oxygenated blood to virtually all tissues · contains the aortic semilunar valve to prevent backflow into the left ventricle

items.name: Ascending Aorta
items.description: extends upward from the heart (~5 cm).

items.name: Aortic Arch
items.description: curves leftward; ends between the 4th and 5th thoracic vertebrae.

items.name: Thoracic Aorta
items.description: descending aorta above the diaphragm.

items.name: Abdominal Aorta
items.description: descending aorta below the diaphragm; terminates at the 4th lumbar vertebra where it bifurcates.

items.name: Aortic Arch Branches (3)
items.description: brachiocephalic artery (branches into right subclavian and right common carotid), left common carotid artery, left subclavian artery.

items.name: Subclavian Artery Branches
items.description: internal thoracic (thymus, pericardium, anterior chest wall), vertebral (brain and spinal cord), thyrocervical (thyroid, neck, upper back, shoulder).

items.name: External Carotid Artery
items.description: supplies face, lower jaw, neck, esophagus, larynx.

items.name: Internal Carotid Artery
items.description: supplies brain; contains carotid sinus with baroreceptors and chemoreceptors.

items.name: Blood Supply to the Brain
items.description: internal carotid and vertebral arteries are the primary suppliers; they form the arterial circle (circle of Willis) for uninterrupted blood supply.

groups.name: Arteries and Veins of the Body (Diagram Labels)

items.name: Arteries: Head, Neck and Chest
items.description: vertebral, right and left common carotid, right and left subclavian, brachiocephalic trunk, aortic arch, ascending aorta, descending aorta, pulmonary trunk, axillary.

items.name: Arteries: Abdomen and Pelvis
items.description: celiac trunk, renal, superior mesenteric, gonadal, inferior mesenteric, common iliac, internal iliac, external iliac.

items.name: Arteries: Arms
items.description: brachial, radial, ulnar, palmar arches.

items.name: Arteries: Legs
items.description: femoral, deep femoral, descending genicular, popliteal, anterior tibial, posterior tibial, fibular, dorsalis pedis, plantar arch.

items.name: Veins: Head, Neck and Chest
items.description: external jugular, internal jugular, subclavian, brachiocephalic, superior vena cava, intercostal.

items.name: Veins: Abdomen and Pelvis
items.description: hepatic, inferior vena cava, renal, gonadal, lumbar, right and left common iliac, external iliac, internal iliac.

items.name: Veins: Arms
items.description: axillary, cephalic, brachial, basilic, median cubital, radial, median antebrachial, ulnar, palmar venous arches, digital.

items.name: Veins: Legs
items.description: femoral, deep femoral, great saphenous, popliteal, small saphenous, fibular, anterior tibial, posterior tibial, plantar venous arch, dorsal venous arch.

groups.name: Development of Blood Vessels and Fetal Circulation

items.name: Early Development
items.description: heart beats by day 21 post-fertilization; circulation patterns established by the fourth week; circulation starts outside the embryo about 15–16 days after fertilization.

items.name: Vascular Development
items.description: arises from embryonic mesoderm; hemangioblasts form angioblasts and stem cells; blood islands form tubes that connect to the heart.

items.name: Placenta
items.description: facilitates nutrient and gas exchange in the growing embryo.

items.name: Umbilical Vein
items.description: carries oxygenated blood from mother to fetus.

items.name: Umbilical Arteries
items.description: transport depleted blood back to the placenta.

items.name: Three Fetal Shunts
items.description: foramen ovale, ductus arteriosus, and ductus venosus. Foramen ovale: right atrium → left atrium · ductus arteriosus: pulmonary artery → aorta, away from the lungs · ductus venosus: shunts blood away from the liver toward the heart

modules.title: Module 5 · The Respiratory System
modules.course: PN Structure and Function of the Human Body · NRSG-10159
modules.topics: Structures · Airways · Lungs and Alveoli · Gas Exchange · Gas Transport · Breathing Mechanics · Control of Breathing

items.name: Breathing Limit
items.description: a typical human cannot survive without breathing for more than 3 minutes; the autonomic nervous system takes control if you hold your breath too long.

items.name: Cellular Respiration
items.description: every cell needs to run the oxidative stages of cellular respiration, the process by which energy is produced in the form of ATP (adenosine triphosphate).

items.name: Main Drive to Breathe
items.description: although oxygen is a critical need for cells, it is the accumulation of carbon dioxide that primarily drives your need to breathe (a negative feedback system).

items.name: O₂ Path
items.description: atmosphere → airways → alveoli → pulmonary capillaries → blood → tissues → cells; CO₂ follows the same path back out.

items.name: Key Idea
items.description: the lungs and blood work as a team: air movement + gas exchange + transport. Respiration keeps cells supplied with O₂ so they can make ATP.

groups.name: Structures and Functions of the Respiratory System

items.name: Major Respiratory Structures
items.description: nasal cavity; pharynx and larynx; trachea and bronchi; lungs; diaphragm and intercostal muscles.

items.name: Primary Functions
items.description: gas exchange (oxygen intake, carbon dioxide removal) and ventilation.

items.name: Secondary Functions
items.description: regulation of blood pH, protection and filtration, sound production, olfaction (smell).

items.name: Conducting Zone
items.description: warms, humidifies and filters air and transports it to the lungs. Nose and adjacent structures, pharynx, larynx, epiglottis, trachea, bronchial tree, terminal bronchiole

items.name: Respiratory Zone
items.description: begins with the respiratory bronchioles and includes alveolar ducts, sacs and alveoli for gas exchange with the blood. Site of gas exchange

items.name: Olfactory Receptors
items.description: located in the mucosa on the superior surface of the nasal cavity.

items.name: Respiratory Mucosa
items.description: lines the rest of the nasal cavity; moistens air and traps incoming foreign particles.

items.name: Conchae
items.description: projections on the lateral walls of the nasal cavity; increase surface area and air turbulence.

items.name: Palate
items.description: separates the nasal cavity from the oral cavity. Anterior hard palate (bone) · posterior soft palate (muscle)

items.name: Paranasal Sinuses
items.description: cavities within bones surrounding the nasal cavity: frontal, sphenoid, ethmoid, and maxillary bones.

items.name: Function of the Sinuses
items.description: lighten the skull; act as resonance chambers for speech; produce mucus that drains into the nasal cavity.

items.name: Pharynx
items.description: muscular passage from nasal cavity to larynx. The oropharynx and laryngopharynx are common passageways for air and food.

items.name: Nasopharynx
items.description: superior region behind nasal cavity.

items.name: Oropharynx
items.description: middle region behind mouth.

items.name: Laryngopharynx
items.description: inferior region attached to larynx (also called hypopharynx).

items.name: Tonsils
items.description: part of the body's immune system; can stop germs entering through the mouth or nose; contain many white blood cells.

items.name: Pharyngeal Tonsil (Adenoids)
items.description: in the nasopharynx.

items.name: Palatine Tonsils
items.description: in the oropharynx.

items.name: Lingual Tonsils
items.description: at the base of the tongue.

items.name: Larynx
items.description: routes air and food into proper channels; plays a role in speech. Made of eight rigid hyaline cartilages and a spoon-shaped flap of elastic cartilage (epiglottis)

items.name: Thyroid Cartilage
items.description: largest hyaline cartilage; protrudes anteriorly (Adam's apple).

items.name: Epiglottis
items.description: superior opening of the larynx; when you swallow, it covers the top of the larynx so food and fluid go into the esophagus.

items.name: Vocal Cords (Vocal Folds)
items.description: vibrate with expelled air to create sound (speech).

items.name: Glottis
items.description: opening between vocal cords.

items.name: Trachea
items.description: connects larynx with bronchi; walls are reinforced with C-shaped hyaline cartilage. Slide activity: palpate your throat to feel the tracheal cartilage.

items.name: Ciliated Mucosa (Trachea)
items.description: cilia beat continuously in the opposite direction of incoming air, expelling mucus loaded with dust and other debris away from the lungs.

items.name: Lungs
items.description: occupy most of the thoracic cavity.

items.name: Apex (Lung)
items.description: near the clavicle (superior portion).

items.name: Base (Lung)
items.description: rests on the diaphragm (inferior portion).

items.name: Lobes
items.description: each lung is divided into lobes by fissures: left lung – two lobes; right lung – three lobes. Left lung has a cardiac notch for the heart.

items.name: Respiratory Tree Divisions
items.description: primary (main) bronchi → secondary (lobar) bronchi → tertiary (segmental) bronchi → bronchioles → terminal bronchioles.

items.name: Terminal Bronchioles
items.description: most distal segment of the conducting zone.

items.name: Bronchioles
items.description: smallest branches of the bronchi.

items.name: Function of Bronchi and Alveoli
items.description: to distribute air to the lung's interior.

items.name: Respiratory Zone Structures
items.description: respiratory bronchioles, alveolar duct, alveoli; site of gas exchange.

items.name: Structure of Alveoli
items.description: alveolar duct → alveolar sac → alveolus.

items.name: Alveoli
items.description: tiny sacs in the lungs where gas is exchanged during breathing; about 150 million alveoli per lung.

items.name: Alveolar Wall
items.description: simple squamous epithelial tissue; a single layer allows oxygen and carbon dioxide to pass quickly from alveoli to capillary.

items.name: Pulmonary Capillaries
items.description: cover external surfaces of alveoli; allow gases to cross by simple diffusion. O₂ is picked up by the blood for transport; CO₂ is released into the air of the alveoli.

items.name: Respiratory Membrane (Air-Blood Barrier)
items.description: alveolar epithelium + fused basement membranes + capillary endothelium; the barrier gases diffuse across.

items.name: Alveolar Pores (Pores of Kohn)
items.description: openings between neighbouring alveoli (shown on diagram).

items.name: Macrophages
items.description: add protection in the alveoli.

items.name: Surfactant
items.description: a slippery coating made by type II alveolar cells; coats gas-exposed alveolar surfaces.

items.name: What It Does
items.description: reduces surface tension so alveoli do not easily collapse (keeps alveoli from collapsing).

items.name: Why It Matters
items.description: makes inhalation easier and supports effective gas exchange. Without surfactant, breathing becomes much harder.

items.name: Clinical Connection
items.description: premature infants may have low surfactant because their lungs are not fully mature.

items.name: Pulmonary (Visceral) Pleura
items.description: covers the lung surface.

items.name: Parietal Pleura
items.description: lines the walls of the thoracic cavity.

items.name: Pleural Fluid
items.description: fills the area between layers of pleura (pleural cavity) to allow gliding.

items.name: Ventilation (V)
items.description: air reaches the alveoli. Example of ↓ ventilation: airway narrowed or blocked, such as during an asthma attack

items.name: Perfusion (Q)
items.description: blood reaches the alveoli. Example of ↓ perfusion: blood flow is reduced, such as with a pulmonary embolus

items.name: 1. Pulmonary Ventilation
items.description: moving air in and out of the lungs.

items.name: 2. External Respiration
items.description: gas exchange between pulmonary blood and alveoli (alveoli ↔ blood).

items.name: 3. Respiratory Gas Transport
items.description: transport of oxygen and carbon dioxide via the bloodstream.

items.name: 4. Internal Respiration
items.description: gas exchange between blood and tissue cells in systemic capillaries (blood ↔ tissues).

items.name: 5. Cellular Respiration
items.description: cells make ATP.

items.name: Clinical Language
items.description: a patient can be moving air but still have poor gas exchange if alveoli, blood flow, or hemoglobin are impaired.

items.name: Gas Exchange
items.description: gas crosses the respiratory membrane by diffusion: oxygen enters the blood; carbon dioxide enters the alveoli. Capillaries are located next to the alveoli to facilitate gas exchange between the respiratory and circulatory systems.

items.name: External Respiration (diagram)
items.description: in the lungs, O₂ moves from the alveolus into the blood and binds hemoglobin; CO₂ is detached from hemoglobin, released from plasma, and converted back from bicarbonate, then moves into the alveolus.

items.name: Internal Respiration (diagram)
items.description: in the tissues, O₂ is detached from hemoglobin and moves into tissue cells; CO₂ moves from tissue cells into the blood.

items.name: Oxygen Transport
items.description: most oxygen travels attached to hemoglobin inside red blood cells ("hemoglobin is the oxygen taxi"). Infographic: hemoglobin carries about 98.5% of O₂; a small amount dissolves in plasma

items.name: Carbon Dioxide Transport
items.description: most CO₂ becomes bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻): cells produce CO₂ → blood carries it mainly as HCO₃⁻ → lungs convert it back → CO₂ exhaled. CO₂ + H₂O ↔ H₂CO₃ ↔ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻

items.name: CO₂ and Blood pH
items.description: when CO₂ rises, acid rises, which can lower pH; breathing helps regulate CO₂ and therefore blood pH.

groups.name: The Diaphragm and Why Air Moves

items.name: Diaphragm
items.description: a thin dome-shaped muscle which separates the thoracic cavity (lungs and heart) from the abdominal cavity (intestines, stomach, liver, etc.).

items.name: Diaphragm in Breathing
items.description: draws downward on inhalation; pushes upward on exhalation.

items.name: Air Movement Rule
items.description: air always moves from higher pressure to lower pressure.

items.name: Inhalation
items.description: diaphragm contracts → thoracic volume ↑ → pressure in lungs ↓ → air flows INTO the lungs.

items.name: Exhalation
items.description: diaphragm relaxes → thoracic volume ↓ → pressure in lungs ↑ → air flows OUT of the lungs.

items.name: Tidal Volume (TV)
items.description: air moved in and out during a normal, quiet breath; about 500 mL.

items.name: Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV)
items.description: extra air you can breathe in after a normal inhalation (think: deep breath in). Graph value: 3100 mL

items.name: Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV)
items.description: extra air you can force out after a normal exhalation (think: blow out as much as you can). Graph value: 1200 mL

items.name: Residual Volume (RV)
items.description: air that always remains in the lungs, even after breathing out as much as possible; helps keep the alveoli open. Graph value: 1200 mL

items.name: Total Lung Capacity (TLC)
items.description: the total amount of air the lungs can hold after the deepest possible breath in; TV + IRV + ERV + RV. Graph value: 6000 mL

items.name: Vital Capacity (VC)
items.description: the maximum amount of air you can move in and out; TV + IRV + ERV; does not include residual volume. Graph value: 4800 mL

items.name: Inspiratory Capacity (IC)
items.description: the maximum amount of air you can breathe in after a normal exhalation; TV + IRV.

items.name: Functional Residual Capacity (FRC)
items.description: the air remaining in the lungs after a normal exhalation; ERV + RV.

items.name: Breathing Control Centers
items.description: located in the pons and medulla of the brain.

items.name: Medulla
items.description: contains the dorsal respiratory group (DRG) and ventral respiratory group (VRG); increases rate and depth of breathing when needed.

items.name: Pons (Pontine Respiratory Group)
items.description: contains the pneumotaxic center and apneustic center.

items.name: Phrenic Nerves
items.description: carry nerve impulses that trigger contraction of the diaphragm.

items.name: Intercostal Nerves
items.description: carry nerve impulses to the intercostal muscles.

items.name: What Stimulates the Control Centers
items.description: CO₂ increase in blood (acts directly) and nerve impulses from O₂ sensors indicating an O₂ decrease. O₂ sensor in artery (aortic arch)

groups.name: Factors Influencing Respiratory Rate and Depth

items.name: Physical Factors
items.description: increased body temperature, exercise, talking, coughing.

items.name: Volition
items.description: conscious control.

items.name: Emotional Factors
items.description: emotions can change breathing rate and depth.

items.name: Carbon Dioxide Levels (Chemical)
items.description: the main regulatory chemical for respiration; increased CO₂ increases respiration; changes in CO₂ act directly on the medulla oblongata.

items.name: Oxygen Levels (Chemical)
items.description: changes in oxygen are detected by chemoreceptors in the aorta and carotid artery; information is sent to the medulla oblongata.

items.name: Homeostatic Feedback Loop
items.description: the regulation of ventilation is part of a homeostatic feedback loop.

items.name: Chemoreceptor Response
items.description: increased CO₂ or decreased O₂ stimulates chemoreceptors, leading to faster and deeper breaths.

items.name: When CO₂ Falls
items.description: ventilation slows to maintain balance.

items.name: Loop Steps
items.description: CO₂ rises in blood → H⁺ rises, pH falls → chemoreceptors detect change → medulla increases rate/depth → more CO₂ is exhaled → CO₂ and pH move back toward normal.

items.name: Nursing Connection
items.description: changes in respiratory rate can be the body trying to correct CO₂ and pH imbalance.

items.name: Muscles Work Harder
items.description: skeletal muscles use more ATP, so they need more oxygen.

items.name: More CO₂ Is Produced
items.description: active cells produce more carbon dioxide as a waste product.

items.name: Response
items.description: respiratory rate and depth increase → more O₂ delivered, more CO₂ removed → homeostasis maintained.

items.name: Hyperpnea
items.description: increased depth and rate of breathing; during exercise it is appropriate because it meets increased cellular demand.

items.name: Fetal Life
items.description: lungs are fluid-filled; placenta handles gas exchange.

items.name: Late Pregnancy
items.description: surfactant production increases as lungs mature.

items.name: Birth
items.description: first breaths expand alveoli; fluid begins to clear.

items.name: After Birth
items.description: pulmonary blood flow increases; lungs take over gas exchange.

items.name: Key Takeaway
items.description: before birth, the placenta oxygenates blood; after birth, the lungs must inflate and exchange gases. Surfactant helps alveoli stay open after the first breaths.

items.name: Apnea (Apnoeic Events)
items.description: temporary stop in breathing.

items.name: Dyspnea
items.description: difficult or laboured breathing.

items.name: Cyanosis / Cyanotic
items.description: bluish colour of the skin or mucous membranes from low oxygen in the blood.

items.name: SOB
items.description: shortness of breath.
